item.title: Quantum could solve AI energy drain, says tech founder
item.description: Quantum computers could curb the vast energy demands of artificial intelligence data centers with their ability to run complex calculations, one of the tech's pioneers told AFP.

item.title: Atomic defects leave telltale optical fingerprints in quantum material
item.description: The tiny atomic defects so important for future quantum technologies can be difficult to spot. Fortunately, they leave behind some clues. The defects can alter how a material responds to light, producing a distinctive optical fingerprint that scientists can measure. The challenge is figuring out which fingerprints belong to which defects.

item.title: Quantum interference keeps two atoms bound despite enough energy to break apart
item.description: How can something remain intact when it should naturally break apart? This question has been addressed by researchers at RPTU. Their work has led to the experimental observation of an unusual quantum state in which two atoms remain bound together even though they possess enough energy to separate. The results have been published in the journal Nature Physics.

item.title: Record-breaking, fast-spinning magnet could help uncover new physics
item.description: A magnet barely wider than a human hair is one of the fastest spinning objects ever and could be useful for both fundamental physics experiments and in quantum technology

item.title: Upgraded microscope can now watch individual quantum particles in motion
item.description: Energy can be carried in a number of ways: by electrons, the particles that underpin all modern electronics, as well as by quasiparticles, the results of different particles interacting with one another at the quantum level. Columbia chemist Milan Delor has been watching these different forms of energy flow with an instrument called stroboSCAT, a unique microscope that uses strobe-like light pulses to capture particles and quasiparticles as they move through different materials.

item.title: New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts
item.description: By injecting “thoughts” directly into large language models, researchers are trying to map out AI’s capacity for introspection. The post New Research Tests Whether AI Models Know Their Own Thoughts first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Quantum gas microscope reveals individual atoms in first tunable three-component Hubbard system
item.description: For the first time, an international team of researchers from Germany, Thailand, India, China and the United States has created a three-component Hubbard system with tunable interactions in the laboratory. In doing so, the team used a quantum gas microscope to make the individual atoms visible. The study, published in Science, provides an important foundation for future quantum simulations of nuclear physics and materials science.

item.title: ‘Reverse physics’ could help bridge the classical and quantum worlds
item.description: Physics is generally built on observations, then the maths that supports them comes later. Columnist Karmela Padavic-Callaghan takes a look at an effort to reverse this and rebuild the laws of physics from the maths up

item.title: Laser-driven magnetic state defies equilibrium rules
item.description: Researchers at the Department of Energy's (DOE's) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and their collaborators used lasers and neutrons to observe a long-lived quantum state in a magnetic material, opening a new way to study materials systems driven far from their equilibrium. Manipulation of quantum magnets is important for advancing quantum information science and could reduce loss of transported information, improve memory devices and benefit other quantum technologies.

item.title: Changing magnetic dimensionality boosts spin-wave frequency in Cr₂₋δTe₂
item.description: Magnons are quasiparticles that represent quantized spin waves in magnetic materials. They can carry information without moving electric charge, making them promising for future information technologies that could use less energy than conventional electronics. The frequency, stability and propagation distance of these waves are all important for their potential applications.

item.title: The Case for a Bubble at Life’s Start
item.description: Is self-enclosure life’s greatest trick? According to the lipid-first theory, a cell membrane enabled life by giving chemistry a place to gather. The post The Case for a Bubble at Life’s Start first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: World's most sensitive lab-based axion search presents its first results
item.description: Physicists at the ALPS II collaboration have reported the first results from the Any-Light-Particle-Search (ALPS) II experiment: the most sensitive instrument of its kind in the search for hypothetical "axions." Headed by Axel Lindner at the DESY Research Centre in Germany, the collaboration found no evidence for axions in this initial campaign, but its results offer valuable guidance for future runs: tightening the search for one of the most promising candidates for dark matter.

item.title: How neutrinos are beginning to reveal the secrets of our galaxy
item.description: Columnist Chanda Prescod-Weinstein says understanding neutrinos is one of the most pressing scientific issues in physics. She shares the latest neutrino discoveries that are exciting her and that could bring us new insights about the galactic centre

item.title: Light-pulse pairs reveal the femtosecond decay of an inner-shell hole in xenon atoms
item.description: Researchers at the UVSOR Synchrotron Facility (Institute for Molecular Science, Japan) and partner institutions have observed the decay of a xenon 4d core hole, an inner-shell vacancy, directly in the time domain. They used pairs of phase-coherent extreme ultraviolet pulses from a synchrotron to make the photoelectron wave packets they released interfere. The contrast of the interference fringes decreased over a few femtoseconds as the delay between the pulses increased. A model using literature

item.title: Barium titanate's optical properties emerge more clearly after decades of widely varying measurements
item.description: A KAIST-led research team has characterized how light propagates through and is absorbed by barium titanate (BTO), a promising material for next-generation optical communication devices. By clarifying optical properties that had been difficult to determine because of the material's complex internal structure, the study provides a foundation for designing these devices.

item.title: New perovskite system extends room-temperature spin polarization via successive quantum wells
item.description: A research team led by Lu Haipeng, a professor in the Department of Chemistry at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), has achieved a breakthrough in preserving spin information for optoelectronic technologies. The team has developed a perovskite chiral multiple quantum-well system that maintains spin polarization approximately 300 times longer at room temperature. The study opens new possibilities for future quantum technologies and next-generation spin-based applications.

item.title: Light reflecting within thin films can masquerade as molecular signals in perovskite solar materials
item.description: An infrared signal thought to reveal how molecules in perovskite solar materials respond to light-generated charges can arise largely from the way light travels through the thin film itself, a new theoretical study shows. item.title: High-pressure setup unlocks detailed measurements of organized structures in turbulent flows
item.description: Turbulent flows are ubiquitous: they are found in clouds, in the ocean and even on other planets. Yet despite their chaotic nature, they also form large-scale structures that can be calculated and predicted. For example, while long streaks of clouds may appear orderly from the outside, their interiors are characterized by intense turbulence.

item.title: Chirality of 'trions' illuminates new paths for quantum optics
item.description: Scientists from Tokyo Metropolitan University have discovered that charged states made of two electrons and a positively charged hole (or vice versa) on atomically thin rolls of carbon atoms have a structure-derived "handedness" in how they interact with light. While electron-hole pairs, or "excitons," were known to keep the chirality of the underlying nanotube, the team showed that adding a charge to create "trions" does not change this property.

item.title: Did Life Begin in an RNA World?
item.description: Some believe the earliest life emerged from self-copying molecules that could mutate and even evolve. But that may not have been enough. The post Did Life Begin in an RNA World? first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Is Schrödinger’s cat both dead and alive? No, it’s just haunted by its past
item.description: A radical new approach suggests some of quantum theory’s most bizarre and inexplicable effects might be down to physics failing to account properly for time

item.title: Weird ‘ultraquantum’ turbulence seen for the first time
item.description: An experiment with ultracold potassium atoms has revealed details of a type of turbulence that only exists in the quantum realm and relies on odd tangles of stringy whirlpools

item.title: 哈雷：不止于彗星
item.description: 哈雷彗星每隔76年重返地球视线。 精准预测彗星回归的哈雷，对宇宙的探索不止于此。他是一个纯粹的行动派，受好奇心驱使，用一生丈量地球。

item.title: 他们来听相对论，还是来看爱因斯坦？
item.description: 1925 年春天，阿尔伯特・爱因斯坦开启一场长途巡回讲学之旅，先前往阿根廷，之后继续到访乌拉圭与巴西。在这本旅行日记中，这位举世闻名的科学家、人道主义代表人物记下了对所见之人、所到之地的即时观感与深度思考。部分耐人寻味的段落，毫无保留地展现出他对到访东道国的真实看法。 本版完整呈现了爱因斯坦这段为期三个月旅途写下的全部日记，为人们展现了这个科学巨人更为真实复杂的一面。

item.title: 一家新型研发机构的十年：“新”在哪里？
item.description: 一个科学慈善、科技创新与全球健康交织的中国故事，以及一家新型研发机构的机制探索。

item.title: 孕期“嘴馋”，大脑里发生了什么？
item.description: 最新研究显示，怀孕会增强小鼠大脑血清素神经元内一种名为SK3的钾离子通道的活性，使参与抑制食欲的神经元变得不那么活跃，进而让孕鼠更容易出现对高热量食物的渴求。

item.title: 人类数学家的反击：N-S方程证明正确性存疑
item.description: OpenAI宣称解决纳维-斯托克斯方程（Navier-Stokes equations，简称N-S方程）问题近两个月后，数学界仍未就OpenAI是否真正解决这一问题达成共识。截至11月2日，N-S方程问题在克雷研究所官网上尚未被列为“已解决问题”。

item.title: 为什么大型犬比小型犬老得更快？
item.description: 最新研究显示，一种负责抑制“跳跃基因”活动的调控机制，随着大型犬年龄增长而减弱得更明显。这可能与大型犬衰老更快、寿命更短有关。

item.title: 香格里拉，曾经是什么模样？
item.description: 1933年，英国作家詹姆斯·希尔顿（James Hilton）在其小说《消失的地平线》（Lost Horizon）中，描述了一个名叫“香格里拉”的世外桃源。

item.title: 一位教授来信：这所高校“顶风作案”，把教师推到KPI传送带
item.description: 2026年10月9日，《中共中央 国务院关于发展新质生产力的意见》（下称“意见”）正式发布。其中第十九条写得明白而具体：“加快推动科研人员考核评价激励与报项目、发论文、评奖励等适度脱钩，防止简单按人才帽子定薪酬、定职称、定待遇。”
